comparisons.interpretation: Both excerpts support universal health care. Rabb specifies Medicare for All as the mechanism; Street's retained statement supports universal coverage without specifying the same mechanism.

Both candidates explicitly characterize health care as a right. Ahmed's surrounding answer supports Medicare for All; Morrison's questionnaire focuses on Medicaid and HIV-service protections. Morrison's source timing is unverified, so this comparison preserves the statement but is not independently established as pre-primary evidence.

Both excerpts seek broad health coverage, but Ruzevich specifies a single-payer Medicare for All model while Casten emphasizes strengthening and expanding ACA coverage. Casten's excerpt does not explicitly oppose Medicare for All, so this is not coded as explicit disagreement.

Ahmed calls for Medicare for All; Tully proposes consolidating coverage into one public payor with optional private supplements. Both support a public-payer model, without establishing identical eligibility, benefits or financing. Tully's pre-primary source version is unverified.

Ahmed specifies Medicare for All; Dunung emphasizes expanding ACA subsidies and protecting existing coverage. These are different stated approaches, not proof that Dunung opposes Medicare for All. Her exact pre-primary version is unverified.
Both explicitly describe healthcare as a human right. That shared principle does not establish the same insurance design; Bankole's pre-primary answer version is unverified.

Ahmed's answer advances Medicare for All; Khot's pre-primary archived platform pledges to protect ACA subsidies. These are different stated approaches, not evidence that Khot rejects other coverage models.

Ahmed calls for Medicare for All while Bean's captured platform emphasizes strengthening the ACA and its subsidies. The excerpts identify priorities, not an explicit vote against the other approach. Bean's pre-primary version is unverified.

Rabb specifies Medicare for All as the route to universal healthcare; Stanford's dated answer calls for a public option alongside drug-price negotiation and cost caps. This compares their stated mechanisms without imputing opposition to an unmentioned proposal.

Rabb specifies a Medicare-for-All financing model. Griffith emphasizes using his Speaker vote as leverage for a floor vote on universal healthcare. Those policy and procedural priorities can coexist; this is not a demonstrated disagreement.
